name: Antique rose
lede: Antique Rose dulls the pink of the rose flower into a muted, slightly brown-grey pink, catalogued by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A faded rose
sections.body:
Rose, the base word, is one of the oldest flower-color names in English; "antique" dulls it toward brown and grey, the way an old dried rose fades [1]. Robert Ridgway recorded this exact shade in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, and the ISCC-NBS system filed it in 1955 under block 19, a grayish red [1][2]. In printed English, use of the phrase "antique rose" rose fastest in the 1990s and peaked in the 2000s, well after Ridgway's plate, so its popularity as a name outran its origin by nearly a century [3]. Its closest named neighbor is [[ash-rose|Ash Rose]], a near-twin at ΔE 4.4 [4], along with [[marsh-rose]] and [[dusty-rose]] [4].

Rose names have multiplied in English since the nineteenth century, as dye and paint catalogs split the flower's pink into ever finer shades: dusty, old, ash and antique among them, each describing a slightly different fade from the fresh flower [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Antique Rose in 92 of 23,781 paintings (0.39 percent, as photographed), rarer than 56 percent of the named colors here [5]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 3.3 times the expected rate for that century, and most often plays an accent color [5]. The earliest matching canvas dates to the year 1000, nine centuries before Ridgway's plate; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a look-alike hue, not the name's actual age [5]. It shows up across a long span of painting history rather than clustering in one movement, which fits a color defined by a wide dye and paint tradition rather than a single workshop or school [5]. As with most of these dulled nature names, the computed match only tells us the hue recurs; it says nothing about whether any painter was reaching for an aged, faded pink on purpose [5].
